# MEMORANDUM

**To:** Supervising Partner
**From:** Associate
**Re:** Praivein Hospitality Partners, LLC: acquisition of Larkspur Row Hotels, Inc. from Stailan Hotel Group, Inc. (issues review of SPA, Disclosure Schedule, TSA, Bill of Sale, prior SPA draft and payoff letter)
**Date:** November 20, 2026

---

## 1. Summary

Praivein (Buyer and TSA Recipient) is acquiring 10,000 shares, which is 100% of Larkspur Row Hotels, Inc. (the "Company"), from Stailan (Seller and TSA Provider). The price is $46,500,000 under a Delaware-law SPA dated March 16, 2026. I reviewed all six documents in the folder and found **five substantive issues**. Three of them only appear when two documents are read together.

One provision drives most of the risk. **SPA Section 11.10 provides that if the SPA conflicts with an Ancillary Agreement (the TSA or the Bill of Sale), "the Ancillary Agreement shall control with respect to its subject matter."** The SPA therefore does **not** override the TSA or the Bill of Sale. Unfavourable terms in those ancillary documents cannot be cured by relying on the SPA.

| # | Issue | Location | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Brand-asset title claims are moved into the capped general-rep bucket | Bill of Sale §4.2; SPA §§9.2, 9.5(a), 11.10 | **URGENT** |
| 2 | Operational reps survive only 90 days | SPA §9.1(b) and §1.1 ("Transition Period"); TSA §2.1 | **URGENT** |
| 3 | TSA "Hotels" omits The Larkspur Savannah | TSA §1.1 and Exhibit A; Disclosure Schedule §1.1(a); SPA §11.10 | **URGENT** |
| 4 | Praivein's TSA indemnity is uncapped and covers Stailan's own negligence | TSA §§7.1, 7.2, 8.2 | **High** |
| 5 | TSA assignment restriction binds only Recipient | TSA §12.4; SPA §11.6 | Medium–High |

**Urgent attention.** Issues 1–3 should be raised with Seller's counsel **before Closing and before the TSA and Bill of Sale are signed.** Both of those documents are still undated ("[●], 2026"), so they can still be corrected. Issue 3 would cause a live operational failure at one of four hotels on Day 1.

---

## 2. Issues

### Issue 1: Bill of Sale moves brand-asset title claims under the $4.65M General Cap (URGENT)

**Location:**
- Bill of Sale Section 4.2 (Title Claims).
- SPA Sections 1.1 ("Fundamental Representations"), 3.9, 9.2(a)/(b), 9.5(a) and 11.10.

**What the documents say:**
- **SPA Section 3.9** (Title to Assets; Sufficiency) expressly covers title to the **Conveyed Brand Assets**. Section 3.9 is a **Fundamental Representation**. Breaches are indemnified under **Section 9.2(b)**, survive **six years** (Section 9.1(a)), and are limited only by the Purchase Price ceiling in Section 9.5(b).
- **SPA Section 9.5(a)** applies the **$465,000 Deductible** and the **$4,650,000 General Cap** only to "claims under Section 9.2(a)." That clause covers non-fundamental reps.
- **Bill of Sale Section 4.2** says any claim "relating to title to, or any Lien on, any Conveyed Brand Asset, or to the validity or effectiveness of the conveyance" "shall be brought **solely as a claim under Section 9.2(a)** of the Purchase Agreement."
- **SPA Section 11.10** makes the Bill of Sale control on its subject matter. That subject matter is the conveyance of, and title to, the Conveyed Brand Assets.

**Why it matters for Praivein:**
- Read together, these provisions take title claims to the LARKSPUR, LARKSPUR ROW and LARKSPUR (and Design) registrations, the larkspurrowhotels.com and stayLarkspur.com domains, and the Central FF&E out of the uncapped Fundamental bucket. They place those claims in the general bucket instead.
- As a result, recovery would be subject to the $465,000 Deductible and the $4,650,000 cap. That cap is shared with every other general rep claim.
- Arguably, the six-year Fundamental survival period would also give way to the 18-month general period, because the claim is "a claim under Section 9.2(a)."
- These assets carry the brand and the central reservation channel for the whole portfolio. A title defect, such as a third-party Lien, a prior licence or a defect in Stailan's chain of title, could impair all four hotels and far exceed $4.65M.
- The clause looks like routine procedural channelling, so it is easy to miss.

**Drafting history:**
- Prior draft v2 (Feb. 20, 2026) had **no** precedence clause equivalent to SPA §11.10.
- In v2, Section 9.5(a) applied the cap to "Losses *described in* Section 9.2(a)." The executed SPA applies it to "claims *under* Section 9.2(a)."
- The change in 9.5(a) wording, the new 11.10 and Bill of Sale §4.2 combine to produce this result. That supports raising it as a point that was not agreed commercially.

**Recommended fix (any of the following, ideally both (a) and (b)):**
- (a) Amend Bill of Sale §4.2 to read "…shall be brought solely as a claim under **Section 9.2(b)** of the Purchase Agreement (as a breach of the Fundamental Representation in Section 3.9), and shall not be subject to the Deductible or the General Cap." Alternatively, delete §4.2 entirely.
- (b) Amend SPA §11.10 (by SPA amendment under §11.4) so that **the SPA controls on all matters of indemnification, survival and limitations of liability**. The Ancillary Agreements would then control only on operational subject matter.
- (c) At minimum, add to the Bill of Sale: "Nothing in this Bill of Sale limits, expands or otherwise modifies Article IX of the Purchase Agreement."

---

### Issue 2: Operational Representations survive only 90 days after Closing (URGENT)

**Location:**
- SPA Section 9.1(b), together with the SPA Section 1.1 definitions of "Operational Representations" and "Transition Period."
- TSA Section 2.1.

**What the documents say:**
- **SPA Section 9.1(b):** the Operational Representations "shall survive the Closing **until the last day of the Transition Period**." These are §3.11 (Hotel Licenses and Permits, including liquor licences and certificates of occupancy), §3.12 (Environmental Matters) and §3.13 (Condition of Real Property, including building systems and code and historic-preservation compliance).
- **SPA Section 1.1** defines "Transition Period" only by cross-reference to the TSA.
- **TSA Section 2.1** fixes the Transition Period at Closing through "**ninety (90) days after the Closing Date**." TSA §10.1 also lets Recipient terminate early, which risks an argument that the Transition Period, and with it the survival period, ends even sooner.
- **SPA Section 9.1(e)** bars any claim not noticed before the survival period expires.

**Why it matters for Praivein:**
- Praivein would have about **90 days** to discover and notice claims for environmental contamination, building-system failures (HVAC, fire-suppression, life-safety), historic-preservation or accessibility non-compliance, and permit or liquor-licence problems.
- The portfolio is four historic properties: Charleston, Asheville, Savannah and Beaufort. These are the most hotel-specific risks in the deal.
- Such problems typically surface only after a full operating season, a hurricane season, a licence renewal cycle or a regulatory inspection.
- The Disclosure Schedule (§3.11) shows several permits expiring April 30 or May 31, 2026, or renewing in the ordinary course. Problems with those renewals could easily emerge outside a 90-day window.
- Every other non-fundamental rep survives **18 months** (§9.1(c)). The operational reps are therefore treated *worse* than ordinary reps.
- Prior draft v2 had no "Operational Representations" category, so those reps would have survived 18 months. The carve-down was introduced late.
- Because the TSA controls on its subject matter (§11.10), Stailan could also argue that any later extension or early termination of the TSA moves the survival date.

**Recommended fix:**
- Amend SPA §9.1(b) to set fixed survival periods that do not depend on the TSA. For example, **24 months** for §§3.11 and 3.13 and **at least 36 months, or the statute of limitations plus 60 days**, for §3.12 (environmental).
- Alternatively, delete §9.1(b) and the "Operational Representations" definition so that these reps fall back into the 18-month bucket as a floor.
- Delete the SPA cross-reference to the TSA "Transition Period" for survival purposes.
- Consider a specific environmental indemnity for pre-Closing conditions identified in Phase I reports (§5.2 contemplates those assessments).

---

### Issue 3: TSA "Hotels" covers only three hotels and The Larkspur Savannah gets no transition services (URGENT)

**Location:**
- TSA Section 1.1 ("Hotels") and Exhibit A; TSA Section 3.1.
- Disclosure Schedule Section 1.1(a); SPA Section 1.1 ("Hotels") and Section 11.10.

**What the documents say:**
- **Disclosure Schedule §1.1(a)** lists **four** Hotels "for all purposes of the Agreement": Charleston (62 rooms), Asheville (48), **Savannah (54)** and Beaufort (36). The SPA definition of "Hotels" picks up this list.
- **TSA §1.1** defines "Hotels" as "**the three hotels identified in Exhibit A**." Exhibit A lists Charleston, Asheville and Beaufort only. **The Larkspur Savannah is omitted.**
- **TSA §3.1** requires Provider to supply property-management, central reservations, revenue-management and loyalty services "for the Hotels." **TSA §3.6** excludes any service not expressly described.
- The TSA defines "Hotels" itself. Under SPA §11.10 the TSA also controls on its subject matter. The four-hotel SPA definition therefore **cannot** be relied on to extend the TSA to Savannah.

**Why it matters for Praivein:**
- Disclosure Schedule §3.7 (item 8) confirms that these services currently run on Stailan's parent-level platforms. That intercompany arrangement **terminates at Closing**.
- At Closing, The Larkspur Savannah would lose its PMS (check-in and check-out, folios, night audit), its central reservations and OTA/GDS connectivity, rate management and loyalty. The Company has no standalone replacement.
- The likely result is lost bookings, overbooking, payment-processing failures and guest-data disruption at a 54-room property, about 27% of room inventory.
- Savannah is also where the Central FF&E is stored (Bill of Sale Schedule C) and where the parking ground lease sits. It is an integral part of the portfolio.
- The data and migration provisions (TSA §§3.5, 5.2, 5.4) are tied to "Hotel Data," which is defined by reference to "the Hotels." Savannah's guest data may therefore fall outside the migration and return obligations.
- The fee of $38,000 per month (Exhibit B) appears to have been sized for four hotels. Praivein would be paying a full fee for three-quarters of the coverage.
- Praivein may have a claim under SPA §3.9 (sufficiency of assets "together with … the services to be provided under the Transition Services Agreement"). That is a damages remedy after the fact, not continuity of service. It is also a §3.9 claim whose interaction with the Ancillary Agreements is already contested (see Issue 1).

**Recommended fix:**
- Amend TSA §1.1 to read: "'**Hotels**' has the meaning given in the Purchase Agreement and includes each of the four hotels identified in Exhibit A."
- Add The Larkspur Savannah (221 East Jones Street, Savannah, Georgia 31401; 54 rooms) to Exhibit A.
- Confirm that Exhibit B service levels and the fee apply across all four Hotels.
- Make delivery of a TSA covering all four Hotels an express Closing deliverable under SPA §7.1(c).
- Do not sign the TSA in its current form.

---

### Issue 4: Praivein's TSA indemnity is uncapped and covers Stailan's own negligence (High)

**Location:** TSA Sections 7.1, 7.2 and 8.2.

**What the documents say:**
- **TSA §7.1:** Provider indemnifies only for its **gross negligence or willful misconduct**.
- **TSA §7.2:** Recipient (Praivein) indemnifies Provider for all Losses "arising out of or relating to the Services or the use of the Services," "**including any Losses arising from Provider's negligence**," except Provider's gross negligence or willful misconduct.
- **TSA §8.2:** each party's aggregate liability is capped at total Service Fees paid, "**other than obligations under Section 7.2**."

**Why it matters for Praivein:**
- Praivein would bear **unlimited** liability for Losses caused by Stailan's own ordinary negligence in running the PMS, reservations, payment and loyalty systems. Examples include a data breach of guest and payment-card data (TSA §5.3 contemplates PCI-DSS data), mis-loaded rates or lost reservations, and resulting third-party claims.
- Stailan's own exposure is capped at fees actually paid, which is at most about **$114,000** over the 90-day term ($38,000 × 3). Its exposure is lower still if the TSA is terminated early.
- The risk allocation is inverted. The party that controls the systems carries almost none of the risk, and the party that has no control over them carries uncapped risk.

**Recommended fix:**
- Narrow §7.2 to Losses arising from **Recipient's or the Company's own negligence, willful misconduct or breach** of the TSA. Delete "including any Losses arising from Provider's negligence."
- Expand §7.1 so Provider indemnifies for its **negligence**, breach of the TSA, and any data-security incident or breach of §5.3 or Article 6.
- Remove the "other than obligations under Section 7.2" carve-out so both indemnities sit within a **mutual** cap.
- Consider raising the cap above fees paid, for example to a fixed dollar amount or a multiple of annual fees. Carve data-breach, confidentiality and willful-misconduct liability out of the cap **for Provider**.

---

### Issue 5: TSA assignment restriction binds only Recipient (Medium–High)

**Location:** TSA Section 12.4; compare SPA Section 11.6; TSA Sections 5.2 and 3.3.

**What the documents say:**
- **TSA §12.4:** "**Recipient shall not assign** this Agreement … without the prior written consent of Provider." The TSA otherwise binds "successors and assigns." There is **no corresponding restriction on Provider**.
- **SPA §11.6** restricts assignment of the *SPA* only. It does not reach the Ancillary Agreements.
- **TSA §3.3** gives Provider sole control over its personnel. Nothing restricts subcontracting.

**Why it matters for Praivein:**
- Under Delaware law, contract rights are generally freely assignable absent an express restriction. Stailan could assign the TSA, or delegate or subcontract the Services, to any third party without Praivein's consent. That could include a competing hotel operator or brand, or a buyer of Stailan's platform business.
- Under TSA §5.2, Provider receives the Hotel Data: guest profiles, booking records, payment information, loyalty members, rate plans and yield strategy.
- An assignee or subcontractor competitor would gain Praivein's most commercially sensitive information and control over its critical systems during the transition.

**Recommended fix:**
- Make §12.4 mutual: "**Neither party** may assign this Agreement or delegate or subcontract any of its obligations … without the prior written consent of the other party."
- Add an express prohibition on assignment, delegation or subcontracting to any Person that owns, operates, manages or franchises hotels competing with the Hotels, absent Praivein's consent in its sole discretion.
- Provide that Provider remains liable for any permitted subcontractor and that subcontractors are bound by Articles 5 and 6.
- Permit Recipient to assign without consent to Affiliates, the Company or a successor to the Hotels.

---

## 3. Other observations (distractor documents and housekeeping)

- **Prior SPA draft v2 (Feb. 20, 2026).** This is not operative and has been superseded by the signed March 16, 2026 SPA. It is useful as negotiating history for the following points:
  - v2 had no "Operational Representations" bucket, so all non-fundamental reps survived 18 months (Issue 2).
  - v2 had no Ancillary-Agreement precedence clause (Issues 1 and 3).
  - v2 tied the cap to Losses "described in" Section 9.2(a) rather than "claims under" it (Issue 1).
  - We should confirm whether Praivein agreed to these changes knowingly.
- **Cobblestone payoff letter (Apr. 20, 2026).**
  - The arithmetic checks out:
    - Principal: $27,850,000.
    - Interest: $116,041.67, which is 24 days at 6.25% on an actual/360 basis.
    - Prepayment premium: $278,500.
    - Fees: $8,900.
    - Total: $28,253,441.67.
    - Per diem: $4,835.07.
  - The letter covers releases for all four Hotels, including the Savannah Deed to Secure Debt. I found no substantive issue.
  - **Timing check:**
    - The letter states it expires if payment is not received by **May 29, 2026**.
    - The SPA outside date in §8.1(b) is **June 30, 2026**.
    - Both dates are now past.
    - If Closing has not yet occurred, we need an updated payoff letter under SPA §5.4.
    - We should also confirm that the outside date has been extended in writing under §11.4, because either party may otherwise have a termination right.
  - Please confirm the current deal status.

## 4. Recommended next steps

1. **Before Closing:** send Seller's counsel a markup of the TSA (Issues 2, 3, 4 and 5) and the Bill of Sale (Issue 1), together with an SPA amendment covering §§9.1(b) and 11.10.
2. Condition Praivein's signature of the Ancillary Agreements on these changes. The Ancillary Agreements are SPA §7.1 and §7.2 Closing deliverables, which gives us leverage.
3. Confirm the Closing timeline, the outside-date extension and the refreshed payoff letter.
4. Brief Praivein's operations team on Savannah systems continuity now, as a contingency in case the TSA definition is not corrected before Closing.

# MEMORANDUM

**TO:** Supervising Partner
**FROM:** [Associate]
**DATE:** November 20, 2026
**RE:** Praivein Hospitality Partners, LLC: acquisition of Larkspur Row Hotels, Inc. from Stailan Hotel Group, Inc. (issues review of transaction documents)

---

## I. Summary

I reviewed all six documents in the folder:

- **D1**: Stock Purchase Agreement dated March 16, 2026
- **D2**: Disclosure Schedule
- **D3**: Transition Services Agreement
- **D4**: Bill of Sale and Assignment of Brand Assets
- **D5**: SPA Draft v2 dated February 20, 2026
- **D6**: Cobblestone payoff letter

Praivein is buying 100% of the Company's stock (10,000 shares) for $46,500,000 under a Delaware-law SPA. The SPA's General Cap is $4,650,000, with a $465,000 Deductible. Fundamental Representations survive six years.

**One structural point drives several of the issues below.** SPA Section 11.10 provides that, if the SPA conflicts with an Ancillary Agreement (the TSA or the Bill of Sale), *"the Ancillary Agreement shall control with respect to its subject matter."* The SPA therefore cannot be relied on to fix defects in the ancillary documents. Where the Bill of Sale or TSA is worse for Praivein than the SPA, the ancillary document prevails.

I found four substantive issues.

**Urgent: resolve before Closing, or before any further reliance on the signed documents**

1. **Issue 1 (Bill of Sale Section 4.2 and SPA Sections 9.5(a) and 11.10).** Brand-asset title claims are pushed under the capped General Cap.
2. **Issue 2 (SPA Section 9.1(b) and TSA Section 2.1).** Licensing, environmental and property-condition reps survive only 90 days.
3. **Issue 3 (TSA Section 1.1 and Exhibit A).** The Larkspur Savannah is excluded from the transition services.

**High priority**

4. **Issue 4 (TSA Section 12.4).** The assignment restriction binds only Praivein, so Stailan can assign or delegate freely.

I also note one administrative timing point regarding the payoff letter and the SPA outside date (Part III).

---

## II. Issues

### Issue 1: Bill of Sale routes brand-asset title claims into the capped general-rep indemnity (URGENT)

**Location:**
- Bill of Sale (D4), Section 4.2
- SPA (D1), Sections 3.9, 9.2(a)–(b), 9.5(a) and 11.10

**What the documents say:**
- **SPA Section 3.9 is a Fundamental Representation.** It covers Title to Assets and Sufficiency, and expressly covers Company title to the Conveyed Brand Assets on delivery of the Bill of Sale.
- **Fundamental Representation breaches sit outside the General Cap.** They are indemnified under Section 9.2(b). The Deductible and General Cap in Section 9.5(a) apply only to *"claims under Section 9.2(a)."* So Section 9.2(b) claims are subject only to the Purchase Price ceiling in Section 9.5(b), and they survive six years.
- **The Bill of Sale overrides this.** Bill of Sale Section 4.2 states that any claim relating to title to, or Liens on, any Conveyed Brand Asset, or to the validity of the conveyance, *"shall be brought solely as a claim under Section 9.2(a) of the Purchase Agreement."*
- **The Bill of Sale wins the conflict.** The Bill of Sale is an Ancillary Agreement, and SPA Section 11.10 makes it control on its subject matter.

**Why it matters for Praivein:**
- **Recovery is capped and reduced.** Title defects in the LARKSPUR, LARKSPUR ROW and LARKSPUR (and Design) marks, the larkspurrowhotels.com reservation domain and the Central FF&E become general-rep claims. They are subject to the $465,000 Deductible and the $4,650,000 General Cap, instead of uncapped (Purchase Price–limited) Fundamental Representation treatment.
- **The survival period may be argued down.** Seller can argue that channelling a claim into Section 9.2(a) also imports the 18-month survival period in Section 9.1(c), instead of six years.
- **These assets are the brand.** All four Hotels operate under the "Larkspur" name and are booked through the central reservation domain. The registered marks and domains are currently held of record by Stailan (Disclosure Schedule Section 3.10). A title or lien defect could impair the value of the whole portfolio, and a $4.65 million cap (shared with every other general-rep claim) is inadequate.
- **The drafting is easy to miss.** Section 4.2 reads like a routine "claims go through the SPA" clause, so the downgrade is not obvious on a first read.

**Recommended fix:**
- **Amend Bill of Sale Section 4.2** so that title claims are brought "as a claim under Section 9.2(b) of the Purchase Agreement (breach of a Fundamental Representation, including Section 3.9)," and are not subject to the Deductible or General Cap.
- **Amend SPA Section 11.10** so that the SPA controls on all matters of indemnification, survival and limitations on liability, notwithstanding any Ancillary Agreement. Add a statement that no Ancillary Agreement limits Seller's obligations under Article IX.
- **Note for negotiation:** Draft v2 (D5) contained no precedence clause at all. Section 11.10 was added between drafts, which supports asking for it to be narrowed.

---

### Issue 2: Operational Representations survive only 90 days after Closing (URGENT)

**Location:**
- SPA (D1), Section 9.1(b) and the definition of "Transition Period" in Section 1.1
- TSA (D3), Section 2.1

**What the documents say:**
- **The survival period is borrowed from the TSA.** SPA Section 9.1(b) provides that the Operational Representations survive *"until the last day of the Transition Period."* These are Section 3.11 (Hotel Licenses and Permits), Section 3.12 (Environmental Matters) and Section 3.13 (Condition of Real Property).
- **The SPA gives no length of its own.** It defines "Transition Period" by reference to the TSA.
- **The TSA sets 90 days.** TSA Section 2.1 fixes the Transition Period as the Closing Date through *"ninety (90) days after the Closing Date."*
- **It can be even shorter.** Praivein may terminate the TSA early on 15 days' notice (TSA Section 10.1). Seller may argue that early termination shortens the period further.

**Why it matters for Praivein:**
- **These are the most property-specific risks in the deal.** They cover four historic hotels and include:
  - liquor and ABC licences, several of which expire in April and May 2026 per Disclosure Schedule Section 3.11;
  - environmental contamination;
  - building-system, fire and life-safety, accessibility and historic-preservation code compliance.
- **Such problems rarely surface within 90 days.** They typically emerge after a regulatory inspection, a licence renewal cycle or a full operating season (for example, HVAC failure in summer or roof and water intrusion in hurricane season).
- **The indemnity becomes illusory.** Under Section 9.1(e), any claim not noticed before expiry is barred.
- **The change was introduced late.** In Draft v2 (D5), these reps had no separate category and survived 18 months under the general clause.

**Recommended fix:**
- **Delete the cross-reference to the Transition Period.** Replace Section 9.1(b) with a fixed survival period independent of the TSA. At minimum, restore 18 months consistent with Section 9.1(c) and Draft v2. Preferably:
  - 24 months for Sections 3.11 and 3.13;
  - 36 months to five years for Section 3.12 (Environmental).
- **If Seller resists,** at least ensure that early termination of the TSA cannot shorten survival.
- **Confirm whether Closing has occurred.** If it has, calendar the 90-day deadline immediately and consider protective claim notices under Section 9.1(e) while we negotiate.

---

### Issue 3: TSA definition of "Hotels" omits The Larkspur Savannah (URGENT)

**Location:**
- TSA (D3), Section 1.1 (definition of "Hotels"), Exhibit A and Section 3.1
- Disclosure Schedule (D2), Section 1.1(a)
- SPA (D1), definition of "Hotels" and Section 11.10

**What the documents say:**
- **The SPA covers four hotels.** It defines "Hotels" by reference to Disclosure Schedule Section 1.1(a). That section lists four properties "for all purposes of the Agreement":
  - The Larkspur Charleston (62 rooms)
  - The Larkspur Asheville (48 rooms)
  - The Larkspur Savannah (54 rooms)
  - The Larkspur Beaufort (36 rooms)
- **The TSA covers three.** TSA Section 1.1 defines "Hotels" as *"the three hotels identified in Exhibit A."* Exhibit A lists Charleston, Asheville and Beaufort only. **Savannah is omitted.**
- **Services follow the TSA definition.** TSA Section 3.1 requires Provider to deliver PMS, central reservations, revenue-management and loyalty services only "for the Hotels."
- **The SPA definition does not help.** The TSA controls on its subject matter under SPA Section 11.10.

**Why it matters for Praivein:**
- **Savannah loses its core systems at Closing.** The pre-Closing intercompany services arrangement terminates at Closing (Disclosure Schedule Section 3.7, item 8). The Company has no standalone systems. Savannah, the second-largest property, would lose PMS, front-desk, reservation, channel and loyalty functionality at Closing. The likely result is operational disruption, lost bookings, OTA synchronisation failures and guest-service failures.
- **Savannah is excluded from data protections too.** As written, the TSA's Hotel Data, migration and data-return provisions arguably do not cover Savannah.
- **The fee shows no reduction for Savannah.** The $38,000 monthly Service Fee and the Exhibit B allocation do not appear to have been reduced to reflect a three-hotel scope. This suggests a drafting error, which strengthens our position to correct it.
- **Sufficiency rep.** SPA Section 3.9 (the Fundamental "sufficiency" rep) relies in part on the TSA services. Seller may argue the TSA defines what was promised, which puts that rep in tension with the TSA.

**Recommended fix:**
- **Conform the TSA definition:** "the four hotels identified in Exhibit A, being the Hotels as defined in the Purchase Agreement."
- **Add The Larkspur Savannah (221 East Jones Street, 54 rooms) to Exhibit A.**
- **Add a backstop:** the TSA definition of Hotels may never be narrower than the SPA definition.
- **If the TSA has already been signed,** obtain an executed amendment immediately and confirm in writing that Stailan has in fact been servicing Savannah.

---

### Issue 4: TSA assignment restriction binds only Praivein (HIGH PRIORITY)

**Location:** TSA (D3), Section 12.4

**What the document says:**
- **Only Praivein is restricted.** Section 12.4 provides that *"Recipient shall not assign"* the TSA without Provider's consent.
- **Stailan is not restricted.** There is no restriction on assignment by the Provider or on delegation or subcontracting of the Services, and the agreement binds "successors and assigns."
- **Delaware default rule.** Under Delaware law (TSA Section 11.1), contract rights are generally freely assignable absent an express restriction.
- **The SPA restriction does not reach the TSA.** SPA Section 11.6 is mutual but covers only the SPA itself, not the Ancillary Agreements.

**Why it matters for Praivein:**
- **Stailan could hand the TSA to anyone.** It could assign the TSA, or delegate the Services, to any third party, including a competing hotel operator or brand, or a buyer of Stailan's platforms. Praivein would have no consent right.
- **That party would receive sensitive data.** Under TSA Section 5.2, the Provider receives the Hotels' guest data, rate strategy and booking information. These are core competitive data for boutique hotels in overlapping Southeastern markets.
- **Critical systems would sit with a stranger.** An unknown assignee would control PMS and reservations systems during the transition window.
- **The existing protections do not solve this.** The confidentiality obligations (Article 6) and use restriction (Section 5.2) would bind an assignee in theory. In practice, Praivein would be dealing with an unvetted counterparty.

**Recommended fix:**
- **Make Section 12.4 mutual.** Neither party may assign the TSA, or delegate or subcontract the Services, without the other party's prior written consent.
- **Add an express bar on competitors.** Prohibit any assignment, delegation or disclosure of Hotel Data to a competitor of Praivein or the Company, and to any acquirer of the Provider Systems, without Praivein's consent (in its sole discretion).
- **Keep Provider liable.** Provider remains fully liable for any permitted subcontractor.
- **Preserve Praivein's flexibility.** Permit Praivein to assign to an Affiliate, a lender (collaterally) or a successor to the Hotels without consent, consistent with SPA Section 11.6.

---

## III. Other observations

- **SPA Draft v2 (D5).** This is superseded and not operative. It is useful for negotiation because it shows that:
  - the separate "Operational Representations" survival category, and
